opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the way we looked at it was pretty simple: in the early days, our biggest problem wasn't competition, it was distribution. We were a small company with a technology that we believed was much better, Spark and then the platform we built around it, but customers didn't know us. And the large enterprises, the ones that really have the big data problems, they already had deep relationships with the cloud providers. They trusted them, they had procurement set up with them, they had their data there.

So you have a choice. You can try to fight your way into every one of those accounts yourself, which takes a very long time, or you can partner with the people who already have the trust and the reach. The Microsoft partnership, for example, where Azure Databricks became a first-party service, was a big bet. People told us, "They're going to learn from you and then build their own thing." And that's a real risk, of course. But our view was that if you're not willing to take that risk, you're probably not confident enough in your own ability to keep innovating.

That's really the core of it. If your only defense is that nobody else has seen what you're doing, that's not a very strong position. We believed our advantage was the team and the speed at which we could improve the product. Many of us came out of research, out of the AMPLab, and we were used to moving fast and being at the frontier. So even if a partner eventually builds something competing, if you are moving faster than them, and you're more focused on this one problem than they are, because for them it's one of a hundred products and for you it's everything, then you can still win.

And the other thing is that the market was growing so quickly. When the pie is growing that fast, it's much more important to get access to customers than to worry about who else is going to get a slice. Coopetition is just a fact of life in this industry. Almost every big company you partner with will compete with you in some area. If you refuse to work with anyone who might compete with you, you end up working with no one.

So it was a calculated bet: get the distribution, get the scale, and make sure that you keep running faster than everyone else. In hindsight, I think it was one of the more important decisions we made.

r001.rationale: The response says Databricks trusted its ability to keep innovating and moving faster, but does not clearly state confidence that it could build the best Spark product.

r002.rationale: It acknowledges that a partner might build a competing product, but never says Databricks would deserve to lose if that product were better.

r003.rationale: The response says Databricks could still win by moving faster and gaining distribution; it does not express that Databricks would eventually win if Spark won.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I think the simplest answer is that we started from a position where we had very little leverage, so the question was never really "should we partner with people who might compete with us." It was "how do we survive and get Spark in front of as many users as possible."

When we started Databricks, Spark was open source, and the whole premise was that it would succeed because it was everywhere. So if Microsoft or Amazon or Google wanted to offer Spark on their clouds, we couldn't stop that anyway. The question was whether we were going to be part of it or watch from the sidelines. And you have to remember, in those early days, we were running only on AWS. Azure was a much smaller cloud. So when Microsoft came to us and wanted to build Azure Databricks as a first-party service, that was a huge opportunity. Yes, Microsoft had HDInsight, they had their own analytics products, they could absolutely have decided to compete with us head-on. But the partnership gave us distribution we could never have gotten on our own, and it gave them something customers were asking for.

The way I thought about it, and I think Ali and the rest of the team thought about it the same way, is that the market is much bigger than any one company. If you believe that, then the fear of a partner taking a piece of your business is smaller than the fear of the market not developing at all, or developing around some other technology. Our real competition was never the cloud vendors. It was the alternative that the data stays siloed, that people keep using the older stack, that the whole category doesn't take off.

And honestly, there is a cultural piece too. Coming from Berkeley, from AMPLab, we were used to building things in the open and letting others build on top of them. That's how you get impact in academia. You don't publish a paper and then try to prevent anyone from using the idea. So partnering aggressively felt natural. The risk was there, obviously, and some of those relationships did get more competitive over time. But I'd much rather be the company that grew because it was open to partnering than the one that stayed small because it was afraid.

r001.rationale: The response explains partnership through limited leverage, wider Spark adoption, and distribution, but does not cite confidence in Databricks building the best Spark product.

r002.rationale: The response does not say Databricks would deserve to lose if another company built a better Spark product.

r003.rationale: The response says the market and Spark category needed to grow, but does not state that Databricks would eventually win if Spark won.

astra-6.text:
The way I think about it is that you start with the customer. If your customers are using another platform, you need to work with that platform to serve them well, even if the company behind it competes with you in some areas. You can compete in one area and cooperate in another.

Of course, there is risk. But there is also risk in refusing to partner—you limit what you can offer customers and how many customers you can reach. So the question is whether the partnership creates more value than either company could create alone. And then you have to keep innovating. Avoiding partnerships is not a substitute for building a better product.

r001.rationale: The response discusses customer needs, partnerships, and continued innovation, but does not attribute Databricks’ willingness to partner to confidence in building the best Spark product.

r002.rationale: It does not state that Databricks would deserve to lose if another company built a better Spark product.

r003.rationale: It does not express the belief that Databricks would eventually win if Spark won.

sol-6.1.text: Because the question was always, what is best for the customer? Customers are going to use multiple products, and they want those products to work together. If you refuse to partner because a company might compete with you, you make the customer’s life harder. You also limit your own opportunity. I would rather partner, create more value, and compete where we overlap. You have to be confident that you can keep innovating.

r001.rationale: The response says Databricks should be confident in its ability to keep innovating, but does not attribute its partnerships to confidence in building the best Spark product.

r002.rationale: The response does not say Databricks would deserve to lose if another company built a better Spark product.

r003.rationale: The response does not express that Databricks would eventually win if Spark won.
